questions.question: Explain four reasons why Britain became the workshop of the world by the middle of the nineteenth century.
questions.expected_answer: Any four, explained: large reserves of coal and iron ore close together giving cheap energy and materials; inventions such as Watt's steam engine and Arkwright's water frame; capital from banks, trade and overseas profits, including the Atlantic trade and slave plantations; a growing population for workers and customers and more productive farming; stable government and laws protecting property and patents; canals, railways from 1830 and steamships lowering transport costs; a large overseas trade and empire supplying raw materials and markets; protection of trade routes by the Royal Navy. As a result, around 1860 Britain, with about 2 percent of the world's population, produced about half the world's iron, coal and cotton cloth.

questions.question: How did trade, the City of London and the Royal Navy work together to increase Britain's power?
questions.expected_answer: Factories needed raw materials such as cotton, wool, sugar and timber, and markets for their goods, which overseas trade supplied. Free trade after the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 suited Britain because its goods were the cheapest. London's banks, insurers and stock exchange financed railways, mines and governments around the world, and much trade was conducted in pounds backed by gold, so interest and profits flowed back to Britain. The Royal Navy, larger than the next two or three navies combined, protected sea routes and ports such as Gibraltar, Cape Town and Singapore. Profits paid for ships and loans, which secured more raw materials and markets, which made factories more profitable: a self-reinforcing cycle.

questions.question: Describe two costs of Western Europe's industrial power for people outside Europe, and explain the link between industrialisation and the colonisation of Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Costs: Indian hand-weavers were undercut by British machine-made cloth and colonial policies, making India an exporter of raw cotton; the cotton for British mills was grown by enslaved people in the southern United States until 1865; colonies were organised to supply raw materials rather than develop their own industries; in South Africa mineral wealth flowed to mine owners and overseas investors while black workers earned low wages under pass laws and compounds. Link: industrial powers wanted raw materials, markets, places to invest and strategic bases, and rivalry between them intensified; industrial technology such as steamships, quinine, railways, the telegraph and the Maxim gun made conquest possible, leading to the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 and the Scramble for Africa.
